summary:
No administrative legal gender recognition procedure is documented for Durango in the vetted sources. Recognition in Mexico is established state by state rather than by a single national statute. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of the 32 states had legislated such a procedure by that date, that two further states operate one in practice without enactment, that six legislatures have enacted nothing, and that only seven states extend recognition to children. The sources reviewed do not identify which of those groups Durango belongs to, so its own legislative position is unresolved. The national framework, not any locally enacted procedure, is the operative rule.

Two superior authorities bind Durango regardless of what its legislature has done. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states in 2022 and extended the right to legal gender recognition to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure across the federation.

Where a state has no procedure, the documented consequence is that document mismatches put trans people at risk at every appearance and every request. Human Rights Watch and the Community Center for Inclusion reported on 6 March 2024 that trans residents of Tabasco without matching identity documents face violence, harassment and humiliation, and are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. Human Rights Watch separately recorded incidents of this kind in Guanajuato.

Lethality and impunity set the background. More than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished in 2022, and impunity for transfemicide is thought higher still. Transgender Europe records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a count second only to Brazil's 100. A trans woman, Karina Gomez, was murdered in Villahermosa in August 2023.

Transfemicide is a defined offence in only two of the 32 states: Nayarit, with sentences up to 60 years, and Mexico City, whose July 2024 statute named for Paola Buenrostro allows up to 70 years. Durango is not documented as having enacted such an offence.

Formal protection and enforcement diverge. Caroline Beer's analysis for LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged national and state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009.
tangentialFactors:
Legal gender recognition in Mexico moves state by state, and the direction of travel over the year to March 2025 was toward adoption. Human Rights Watch reported the same month that many states now operate administrative procedures and called on the six legislatures that have enacted nothing to close the gap, while warning that implementation differs sharply between states. Durango sits inside that distribution, and no reporting reviewed separates its position from the national picture.

The unevenness is measurable in scope as well as count. Only seven states extend recognition to children, so a minor seeking recognition may be refused in most of the federation even where an adult procedure exists.

Two neighbouring-state cases stand as evidence of what silence means rather than as statements about Durango. The Tabasco findings of March 2024 describe trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, with the resulting scrutiny compounding exclusion in banking, health care and dealings with police; the same reporting set those barriers against the murder of Karina Gomez in Villahermosa in August 2023. Guanajuato supplies further recorded incidents of document-driven discrimination.

Violence against trans people intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months.

Transfemicide legislation is a narrow and recent benchmark. Mexico City's Congress passed the Paola Buenrostro law in July 2024, and the city became the second of the 32 states to criminalise transfemicide after Nayarit. The statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.
localsOnly:
Residents of Durango hold recognition rights through rulings that bind the state's authorities rather than through a documented state procedure. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states in 2022 and extended the right to legal gender recognition to minors; the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Whether Durango's own civil registry operates a procedure under those rulings is not documented in the sources reviewed.

Only seven states extend legal gender recognition to children, so families in Durango seeking recognition for a minor depend on the Supreme Court's 2022 extension rather than on local enactment.

Where documents do not match a person's gender presentation or lived identity, the recorded consequences for residents across the affected states are harassment and humiliation at each document request, and exclusion from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. Human Rights Watch documented this pattern in Tabasco and recorded comparable incidents in Guanajuato.

Residents live under a national impunity rate above 95% of homicides in 2022, with transfemicide impunity assessed as higher still. Durango has not been documented as criminalising transfemicide, leaving Nayarit and Mexico City as the only two states with such an offence.

Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009, so partnership recognition does not depend on Durango's legislature.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Durango is one of the six state legislatures that have enacted no legal gender recognition procedure as of March 2025, one of the two states running a procedure in practice without enactment, or among the 22 that have legislated one. No source reviewed places Durango in any of these groups, and the vetted reporting does not name all members of the six.

Unresolved: whether Durango operates any procedure under the Supreme Court's 2022 guidelines, or under an Inter-American Court requirement, in the absence of state legislation. No Durango-specific administrative or judicial reporting was available in the sources.

Unresolved: whether Durango has enacted a transfemicide offence or any hate-crime enhancement applicable to violence against trans people. The transfemicide laws documented are those of Nayarit and Mexico City only, and the sources reviewed do not cover Durango's penal code.

Not sourced: no Durango-specific record of violence against trans people, of police conduct toward trans detainees, or of access to gender-affirming health care was found. The figures cited are national or drawn from other states and are not evidence of conditions inside Durango.

The two states operating procedures in practice without legislation are not named in the reporting reviewed, so comparison of Durango's administrative practice against them is not possible.
